subject: biology
title: Core practicals: plants, microbes and ecology
key_idea: These core practicals cover plant tissues and fibres, mineral deficiencies, antimicrobial tests, field ecology, temperature and development, the Hill reaction and gel electrophoresis. Each is a fair test with controls and safe handling. Know the method, the variables and how to interpret the result.

sections.heading: Plant tissues, fibres and mineral deficiencies

blocks.text: Three core practicals investigate the structure and needs of plants: the tissues in a stem, the strength of fibres and the effect of missing minerals.

items: Cut a thin transverse section of a stem and stain it, for example with toluidine blue, which colours lignin blue-green.
Use a light microscope. Start on low power, then use high power.
**Xylem vessels** are wide, thick-walled tubes with lignin, found in vascular bundles towards the inside of the bundle.
**Phloem sieve tubes** have thinner walls and are found towards the outside of the bundle, next to companion cells.
**Sclerenchyma fibres** have very thick lignified walls and are found in a cap outside the phloem, giving support.
Make a labelled drawing, recording where each tissue is.
Grow seedlings in solutions that lack one mineral each, and compare them with a complete solution as a control.
Nitrate deficiency stunts growth and causes yellow older leaves. Magnesium deficiency causes yellow leaves (chlorosis) as chlorophyll cannot be made.
Control light, temperature, volume of solution, and the number and type of seedlings.
Measure growth with a mean height, leaf area or dry mass, and observe leaf colour.
Aerate the solution, or the roots will lack oxygen.
Hang masses from a fibre until it breaks. Add the mass in equal steps.
Tensile strength is the force a fibre can withstand before breaking, per unit of cross-sectional area.
Use fibres of the same length and thickness, and the same part of the plant, or compare them by the cross-sectional area.
Repeat several times and use a mean.
Fibres from different plants or parts of a plant differ in strength, because of their structure and lignin content.
Use a safety screen or clamp, and keep feet out from under falling masses.
Stain and look at a stem section to find xylem, phloem and sclerenchyma.
Compare deficient plants with a complete solution as a control.

blocks.text: Two practicals test substances against bacteria. Both need aseptic technique to protect the user and the culture.

items: Spread a lawn of bacteria on an agar plate with a sterile spreader.
Place discs soaked in plant extracts or antibiotics on the lawn, with a control disc soaked in sterile water.
Tape the lid on without sealing it, and incubate upside down at around 25 °C. Do not use higher temperatures, which favour pathogens.
A clear zone around a disc is where bacteria have been killed or stopped growing.
A larger clear zone means a more effective substance. Compare using the area, πr², rather than the diameter.
Measure the diameter of each clear zone across the centre of the disc, halve it to get the radius, and take a mean of repeats.

blocks.label: Area of a clear zone
where: r = the radius of the clear zone, in mm

items: Control the concentration of each extract, the volume and size of the disc, the depth of agar, and the incubation time and temperature.
Different antibiotics have different effects, because bacteria differ in cell wall structure, so some are more affected than others.
Take care with a cultured microbe: wash hands, wear gloves, disinfect, and sterilise used plates by autoclaving.
Include a control disc and compare clear zones by their area.
Aseptic technique and incubation at about 25 °C keep the practical safe.

blocks.text: These practicals measure living things in the field or in the lab, and the light reactions in isolated chloroplasts.

items: A **quadrat** is a square frame used to sample plants in a small area. Count the number of individuals or estimate the percentage cover.
Place quadrats at random positions, using random numbers as coordinates, to avoid bias.
A **transect** is a line along which samples are taken, to show how distribution changes across a gradient, such as from a path into woodland. Use quadrats at regular intervals along it.
Measure abiotic factors suited to the habitat, such as light intensity, soil moisture, temperature and pH.
**Abundance** is how many of a species there are; **distribution** is where they are found.
Use enough quadrats to give reliable data, and calculate a mean abundance.
Measure the effect of temperature on growth or development, for example the growth rate of seedlings or the hatching rate of brine shrimp eggs.
Keep the organisms at different temperatures in incubators or water baths, and measure the number hatched or height at set times.
Control the number of eggs or seeds, light, water and salinity.
Development speeds up with temperature, up to an optimum, then falls as enzymes denature.
Chloroplasts are isolated by grinding leaves in cold, buffered, isotonic solution and centrifuging.
The cold keeps enzymes active and slows damage. The buffer holds pH. The isotonic solution prevents osmotic damage.
DCPIP is a blue dye that is reduced, becoming colourless, as it takes up electrons and hydrogen released in the light-dependent reaction.
The time taken or a colorimeter reading shows the rate of the light reaction.
Use controls: chloroplasts in the dark, boiled chloroplasts, and no chloroplasts, to show that light and working chloroplasts are needed.
Random sampling avoids bias; a transect samples along a gradient.
In the Hill reaction, DCPIP loses its blue colour as it is reduced.

blocks.text: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by length, as in DNA profiling.

diagram.alt: Put the steps of gel electrophoresis in order.
diagram.prompt: Put these steps of gel electrophoresis in order.
steps: Cut the DNA into fragments with restriction enzymes
Load the samples into wells at the negative end of the gel
Run an electric current through the gel
Stain the DNA so the bands can be seen
Compare the bands with known fragment sizes

items: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode.
Shorter fragments move faster and further through the gel, so fragments are separated by length.
Include a lane of fragments of known lengths, the DNA ladder, as a comparison.
The buffer conducts current and keeps pH steady. Keep the gel covered with buffer.
Handle the gel and stains safely and wear gloves, because some stains are hazardous.
DNA moves to the positive electrode, with the shortest fragments going furthest.
A ladder lets the lengths of unknown fragments be estimated.

checks.q: In an antibiotic practical, explain why a disc soaked in sterile water is included on the plate.
checks.a: It acts as a control; to show that the paper disc and water do not themselves stop bacterial growth; so any clear zone is due to the antibiotic.

checks.q: A clear zone has a radius of 6 mm. Calculate its area.
Explain why DNA fragments of different lengths are separated during gel electrophoresis.
checks.a: DNA is negatively charged; so moves towards the positive electrode; shorter fragments move through the gel more easily, so travel further in the same time.
